prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Beneath these fruit-tree boughs that shed Their snow-white blossoms on my head, With brightest sunshine round me spread Of spring's unclouded weather, In this sequestered nook how sweet To sit upon my orchard-seat! And birds and flowers once more to greet, My last year's friends together. One have I marked, the happiest guest In all this covert of the blest: Hail to Thee, far above the rest In joy of voice and pinion! Thou, Linnet! in thy green array, Presiding Spirit here to-day, Dost lead the revels of the May; And this is thy dominion. While birds, and butterflies, and flowers, Make all one band of paramours, Thou, ranging up and down the bowers, Art sole in thy employment: A Life, a Presence like the Air, Scattering thy gladness without care, Too blest with any one to pair; Thyself thy own enjoyment. Amid yon tuft of hazel trees, That twinkle to the gusty breeze, Behold him perched in ecstasies, Yet seeming still to hover; There! where the flutter of his wings Upon his back and body flings Shadows and sunny glimmerings, That cover him all over. My dazzled sight he oft deceives, A brother of the dancing leaves; Then flits, and from the cottage-eaves Pours forth his song in gushes; As if by that exulting strain He mocked and treated with disdain The voiceless Form he chose to feign, While fluttering in the bushes.

outputs.L1:
Beneath these fruit-tree boughs, which shed  
Their snow-white blossoms on my head,  
With brightest sunshine round me spread  
Of spring’s unclouded weather,  
In this sequestered nook, how sweet  
To sit upon my orchard seat,  
And birds and flowers once more to greet—  
My friends of last year, all together.

One have I marked, the happiest guest  
In all this covert of the blest:  
Hail to thee, far above the rest  
In joy of voice and pinion!  
Thou, Linnet, in thy green array,  
Presiding spirit here today,  
Dost lead the revels of the May;  
And this is thy dominion.

While birds and butterflies and flowers  
Make all one band of paramours,  
Thou, ranging up and down the bowers,  
Art sole in thy employment:  
A life, a presence like the air,  
Scattering thy gladness without care,  
Too blest with any one to pair—  
Thyself thine own enjoyment.

Amid yon tuft of hazel trees,  
That twinkle in the gusty breeze,  
Behold him perched in ecstasies,  
Yet seeming still to hover;  
There, where the flutter of his wings  
Upon his back and body flings  
Shadows and sunny glimmerings  
That cover him all over.

My dazzled sight he oft deceives—  
A brother of the dancing leaves;  
Then flits, and from the cottage eaves  
Pours forth his song in gushes,  
As if, by that exulting strain,  
He mocked and treated with disdain  
The voiceless form he chose to feign  
While fluttering in the bushes.
outputs.L2:
Under the branches of these orchard trees, pale blossoms drift down upon me. Clear spring sunlight fills the quiet retreat, where I rest on a seat among the fruit trees. Here I happily welcome again the birds and flowers that were my companions the year before.

Among them, one visitor stands out as the most joyful creature in this sheltered paradise. I salute you, linnet, whose song and flight surpass all others in delight. Dressed in green, you rule over this place today, directing May’s festivities as though the whole domain belonged to you.

Birds, blossoms, and butterflies seem joined together like lovers, but you move alone through the leafy shelters, wholly devoted to your own happiness. Like the air itself, you are both a living being and an everywhere-felt presence, freely spreading joy. You are too completely content to need a mate; your pleasure comes entirely from within.

Look toward that cluster of hazel trees, their leaves sparkling as the uneven wind stirs them. The linnet sits there in rapture, though the movement of his wings makes him appear still airborne. As they flutter, shifting patches of brightness and shade play across his back and body until he is covered in flickering light.

He repeatedly confuses my dazzled eyes, looking almost like a companion to the swaying leaves. Then he darts away to the cottage roof and releases his song in sudden, overflowing bursts. His triumphant music seems to ridicule the silent shape he had pretended to be while trembling among the bushes.
outputs.L3:
The speaker delights in sitting beneath blossoming fruit trees, surrounded by the fresh beauty of spring. The return of birds and flowers fills the orchard with renewed life, making the season a time of warmth, color, and celebration. Among all the creatures that visit this peaceful setting, the linnet stands out as the happiest and most joyful presence.

The linnet seems to preside over the festivities of May, freely spreading gladness throughout its natural domain. Perched among the hazel trees as they sway in the wind, the bird flutters its wings, creating shifting patterns of shadow and sunlight. For a moment, it blends almost indistinguishably with the dancing leaves. Then it flies to the cottage eaves, where it pours out an exuberant song that captures the vitality and delight of spring.
outputs.L4:
The speaker stands beneath the blossoming branches of a spring orchard and takes in the beauty and energy of the natural world. White petals hang overhead and drift through the air, while flowers brighten the ground and birds move among the trees. Everything appears animated: branches sway, leaves dance, blossoms fall, and the orchard seems filled with color, motion, and music. Within this lively scene, the linnet becomes the speaker’s chief source of wonder. Its quick movements and cheerful song express the freshness and abundance of the season more perfectly than any other part of the landscape.

The speaker addresses the linnet with admiration, treating it not merely as a small bird but as the living spirit of May. At first it almost disappears into the surrounding foliage, blending with the leaves and branches, yet its voice reveals its presence and fills the orchard with joy. Unlike human happiness, which often depends on recognition, reward, or companionship, the linnet’s delight appears complete in itself. It sings because singing is natural to it, enjoying its own existence without self-consciousness or restraint. In this way, the bird embodies freedom, innocence, and self-sufficient pleasure. Its music gathers together the orchard’s blossoms, flowers, movement, and light, transforming the whole scene into a celebration of spring’s exuberant vitality.

counterfactuals.output:
## “The Green Linnet”  
*William Wordsworth*

Beneath these fruit-tree boughs that shed  
Their snow-white blossoms on my head,  
With brightest sunshine round me spread  
Of spring’s unclouded weather,  
In this sequestered nook how sweet  
To sit upon my orchard-seat  
And birds and flowers once more to greet,  
My last year’s friends together!

One have I marked, the happiest guest  
In all this covert of the blest:  
Hail to Thee, far above the rest  
In joy of voice and pinion!  
Thou, Linnet! in thy green array  
Presiding Spirit here to-day  
Dost lead the revels of the May;  
And this is thy dominion.

While birds, and butterflies, and flowers,  
Make all one band of paramours,  
Thou, ranging up and down the bowers,  
Art sole in thy employment:  
A Life, a Presence like the Air,  
Scattering thy gladness without care,  
Too blest with any one to pair;  
Thyself thy own enjoyment.

Upon yon tuft of hazel trees,  
That twinkle to the gusty breeze,  
Behold him perched in ecstasies,  
Yet seeming still to hover;  
There! where the flutter of his wings  
Upon his back and body flings  
Shadows and sunny glimmerings,  
That cover him all over.

My dazzled sight he oft deceives,  
A Brother of the dancing leaves;  
Then flits, and from the cottage-eaves  
Pours forth his song in gushes;  
As if by that exulting strain  
He mocked and treated with disdain  
The voiceless Form he chose to feign,  
While fluttering in the bushes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
